finding: The child environment list (`TP_RUN_ID`, `TP_UNIT_ID`, `TP_UNIT_KIND`, `TP_UNIT_SEQ`, `TP_ROUND`, `TP_RUN_DIR`, `TP_ROUND_DIR`, `TP_FILE`) carries no phase variable, yet two records a child must write require one: `tp escalate` writes `{decision, unit_kind, unit_id, phase, evidence, options[], at}` (§5.2), and `last_failure` — which §4.2 also says is written when a unit "closes with a failed quality gate", i.e. inside the child's own `tp done` — carries `phase` too. The implementer must invent the source: re-derive the phase by running the oracle inside `tp escalate` (contradicting §3.1.1's stated reason for `TP_FILE`, that a child does not re-run the driver's resolution), or leave it empty.
suggestion: Either add `TP_PHASE` to the spawned environment alongside `TP_ROUND`, or state that `tp escalate` and the gate path derive `phase` from `tp resume` over `TP_FILE` and specify what they record when that derivation fails. Also state, in §4.2, which process writes `last_failure` in each of its two trigger cases (driver on non-zero exit vs. child on gate failure).

finding: The role predicate is "exists and every line parses" (line 181/185) and §6.2 line 438 restates it as "present and wholly parseable", but neither says what a blank or whitespace-only line does — while §8a.4 line 561 explicitly exempts blank lines only for `--merge`'s inputs accounting. NDJSON files normally end with a newline, so a naive line split yields a trailing empty line. Two engineers write contradictory tests: one asserts a role file ending in \n passes the predicate, the other asserts the Stop hook blocks it. Tests 48, 49 and 52 make the collision concrete — test 49 requires `--merge` to exit 0 on a file of only blank lines, while test 48 says a file holding "an unparseable line" fails the predicate, and test 52 requires the oracle, the driver and the hook to agree.
suggestion: State in §3.3 that the predicate ignores blank and whitespace-only lines exactly as §8a.4 does (or that it requires at least one parseable line), and add a test asserting a role file with a trailing newline satisfies the predicate in all three evaluators.

finding: Who writes a unit's `.jsonl` log is unspecified and the two stated mechanisms conflict. §3.5 says "Each unit's runner output streams to `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`" (driver redirects the child's stdout), while §3.2 lists `{log_path}` as a placeholder the runner's own `args` receive — and `TP_RUNNER_SEAM`'s arg template (§3.2.1) passes it, implying the runner writes the file itself. If the driver redirects stdout *and* the runner opens the same path, the two interleave or truncate each other, and "the final line" the spend read depends on (§3.2.2, test 11) becomes undefined. The `claude` template's args contain no `{log_path}` at all, so the two built-ins would need opposite handling that the spec never distinguishes.
suggestion: State one owner: e.g. the driver always creates and redirects the child's stdout to `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, and `{log_path}` is passed only as informational (a runner that also writes it appends, or is documented as unsupported). Say explicitly whether stderr is captured in the same file, and which stream the spend line is read from.

finding: Test 5 (line 605) pins the assertion method — "asserted from the seam's recorded spawn and exit timestamps" — but concurrency cannot be proven from timestamps unless the fake runner is made to overlap: a seam child that exits immediately can produce disjoint intervals even when the driver spawned all roles before waiting, so the test fails intermittently on a loaded machine. Nothing in §3.2.1's seam contract (line 151-158) gives the fake runner a way to block until its siblings have started.
suggestion: Either give the seam a documented synchronisation hook (e.g. the fake runner waits on a rendezvous file until N siblings exist, so overlap is forced rather than observed), or restate test 5 to assert the spawn set — all role children spawned before any wait, and no non-role child spawned in the same iteration — which is decidable from the recorded invocation order alone.

finding: Test 6 (line 607) asserts "a second `tp run` over the same state resumes at the same unit". That holds for `implement` (§3.1.1 line 81) but is false for role units: §3.1.1 line 99 and §4.1 line 308 have the oracle omit any role whose findings file already satisfies the predicate, and test 36 (line 677) explicitly asserts the second run does NOT re-run those roles. A driver killed after a role child finished writing therefore resumes at a different unit. As written, tests 6 and 36 assert opposite outcomes for the same scenario.
suggestion: Restate test 6 as "a second `tp run` resumes at the first unit the oracle still returns, re-running an interrupted unit whose durable write is absent and skipping one whose write is present", so it composes with test 36 instead of contradicting it.

finding: Test 15 and §10.7 fix the `.tp/.gitignore` additions at exactly four entries — `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/`, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json` — but this version introduces a fifth generated path, the run lock at `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock` (§3.1.1), which is not covered. Every `tp run` would then leave an untracked file in the repo, which is exactly the dirty-tree failure a task-closing commit must not produce. The `<base>` entries also need a glob form (`run-*.json`, `last_failure-*.json`) since the base varies per task file, and the test's wording pins literal names.
suggestion: Add `.tp/locks/` to the shipped `.tp/.gitignore`, make test 15 read "five entries" with glob patterns for the per-base files, and update §10.7's "gains four entries".

finding: Nothing states who creates `TP_RUN_DIR`, `TP_ROUND_DIR` and `.tp/locks/`, or with what permissions. §6.3 has `tp review`/`tp audit` emit a path under `$TP_ROUND_DIR` for the child to write, §5.2 has `tp escalate` write into `$TP_RUN_DIR`, and §3.1.1 has the driver delete a role file inside `$TP_ROUND_DIR` before spawning — three writers, no stated creator. If the driver does not `mkdir -p` before the first spawn, every one of those writes fails on a fresh repo; if children create them, a `--dry-run` or a crashed driver leaves the tree in a different state than the same code path assumes.
suggestion: State that the driver creates `.tp/locks/`, `$TP_RUN_DIR` and (in a round-based phase) `$TP_ROUND_DIR` before spawning the iteration's first child, that creation is idempotent, and that children may assume both directories exist.

finding: Two normative claims in §3.2.1 have no test in §10. (a) Line 140: "Every child is spawned with stdin closed" — nothing in 10.1-10.6 asserts it, though the fake runner seam could read stdin and report EOF. (b) Lines 135-137 and 160-162: `--max-budget-usd` is appended only when the resolved `run_max_unit_budget_usd` is non-zero, 0 omits the flag pair for the `claude` template, and a positional template still receives the literal `0`. Test 10 covers only "every placeholder resolves", test 11 only `spend_key`, test 16 only field defaults and ranges — none pins the 0 boundary that the spec calls out twice.
suggestion: Add a test asserting the child's stdin is at EOF, and a test asserting that at `run_max_unit_budget_usd=0` the `claude` template's argv contains no `--max-budget-usd` while a positional template receives a literal `0`, with the non-zero case as the contrast.

finding: `tp run`'s own output is never specified. §3.4 says a caller "separates 'the cycle is done' from 'a human is needed' without parsing the payload", which asserts a payload exists, but only `--status` (§3.5) and `--dry-run` have a described shape. An implementer has to invent what `tp run` prints while looping and what it emits on exit (a JSON object with `stop_reason`? progress lines? nothing?), whether it honours tp's piped-JSON/TTY convention, and where §3.2.2's mandated run-start report of unmetered kinds and §5.2's multi-escalation report are printed.
suggestion: Add a short subsection to §3.5 fixing `tp run`'s final payload (at minimum `{run_id, phase, stop_reason, totals, last_unit}`) under both JSON and TTY, and name the stream and format for progress lines, the run-start unmetered-kinds report, and the escalation report.

finding: §3.4 says caps are evaluated between iterations only and then bounds the consequence to "its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration", omitting `cap-units`. But one iteration spawns every concurrent role unit at once (§3.1 step 4, §3.3), and `run_max_units` counts attempts (§3.4, test 33), so the unit count can overshoot `run_max_units` by up to the number of active roles for the phase — the same class of overshoot the sentence claims applies only to the other two caps.
suggestion: Extend the overshoot sentence to name `cap-units` as well ("a run can overshoot its unit, wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration"), and state the bound explicitly as the iteration's unit count so a test can assert it.

finding: The retry counter has no owner. §3.4 requires a unit to be attempted `1 + run_max_unit_retries` times before `unit-failure`, and the run-state schema carries `attempt` per row — but §3.5 states categorically that run state is "observability, not truth: no decision — the driver's or a hook's — reads it back", which forbids deriving the attempt count from it. §3.1 also says the loop "never holds work in memory that it could re-derive", and §4.2's `last_failure` is explicitly advisory and holds no count. So no section says where the attempt count lives, nor what happens to it across the re-poll of the oracle in §3.1 step 1 or across a driver death.
suggestion: State in §3.4 or §3.1.1 that attempts are counted in driver memory within one run only, that retries happen inside the same iteration (or that the oracle re-returning the same `(kind,id)` continues the count), and that a new run restarts attempts at 1 — the same way §3.5 already says totals restart at zero. Add it to test 8.

finding: §4.1 requires the oracle to omit any role "whose findings file already satisfies §3.3's predicate", which means `tp resume` must open `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r<round>/role-<id>.ndjson`. But that path is introduced in §3.1.1 solely as a value the *driver* computes and exports as `TP_ROUND_DIR`, and §6.2's hook and §6.3's agents both consume it from the environment. Nothing assigns the derivation to a shared owner, so three components construct or consume the path on three different authorities. Test 52 pins that the oracle, driver and Stop hook agree on the *predicate*; nothing pins that they agree on the *path* the predicate is applied to.
suggestion: Name the round-directory layout as a shared derivation (owned by the state layer, used by the oracle and exported by the driver) rather than as a driver-side env var, and extend test 52 to assert the oracle's computed path equals the `TP_ROUND_DIR` the driver exports for the same phase and round.

finding: `last_failure` has two triggers — "a unit exits non-zero, or closes with a failed quality gate" (line 323) — but only the first is observable by the driver; the gate failure happens inside the child, so `tp done` itself must write the record. The spec never says what `unit_kind`, `unit_id` and `phase` hold when `tp done` fails its gate outside a run (no `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID` set), nor whether the record is written at all in that case — unlike `tp escalate`, whose out-of-run behaviour §5.2 line 380 pins explicitly. Test 23 exercises only the non-zero-exit path and asserts nothing about `summary`, which line 324 requires to carry the failing command and the gate's own output.
suggestion: Say whether a gate failure outside a run writes the record and what the identity fields hold there (or declare it a no-op, matching §5.2's out-of-run rule), and extend test 23 to cover the gate branch and assert the tp-authored `summary` content.

finding: Round 14 subordinated escalation to §3.4's precedence so a cycle that became releasable in the same iteration records `converged`. Nothing then carries the escalation: the run exits 0 (§3.4), `notify_cmd` fires only on non-converged stops (§5.2), and §5.2's "the driver reports the lowest `seq`" rule is written for an escalation stop, so a unit that asked for a user-only decision leaves a record on disk that no exit code, notification or status field points at. The pre-repair rule ("the record, not the exit code, is the signal") is exactly what this weakens.
suggestion: State what a converged stop does with escalation records that exist in the same run: keep them in `--status` output (e.g. an `escalations[]` of paths) and/or invoke `notify_cmd` with `TP_ESCALATION_PATH` on a converged stop that has records, so precedence decides `stop_reason` without discarding the operator signal.

finding: The new persistence rule — "A record unit writes that file only when it is absent" — makes presence the sole test for `merged.ndjson`, but no section requires that write to be atomic (§3.5 mandates temp+rename for run state only). A record unit killed mid-write leaves a truncated `merged.ndjson`; §3.1.1 forbids deleting it, so the retry re-records from the corrupt file forever, and §3.3's `review-record` predicate ("merged.ndjson … exists") reports it satisfied. The very crash-resumption case the repair was written for is the one it cannot recover.
suggestion: Require the merge write to be atomic (temp + rename) so presence implies completeness, or make the persistence condition "present and wholly parseable" — the same predicate §3.3 already uses for role files — so a truncated merge is rewritten rather than inherited.

finding: The reviewer/auditor agents "may write exactly one path … and are denied every other write" (test 55 asserts the denial), but a role unit must run `tp review`/`tp audit` and `tp escalate`, which requires a shell tool — and §6.2 states shell tools are deliberately outside the write matcher. With a shell permitted, no path-scoped denial holds, so test 55's "deny every other path" is unachievable as stated. The spec also never says through which mechanism the path allowlist is expressed: an agent definition restricts *tools*, not paths, so path scoping needs permission rules or another `PreToolUse` matcher that §6.2's table does not list.
suggestion: Scope the claim to what is enforceable: name the mechanism (agent `tools` list plus a permission/`PreToolUse` rule) and restate the guarantee as "denied every other write through the file-writing tools", matching §5.1's honest fence-not-sandbox framing. Reword test 55 to assert the tool-level denial, not an absolute one.

finding: §6.4 requires every shipped hook to "exit non-zero rather than hanging" on its 10-second timeout, but for the `Stop` hook a non-zero exit is precisely the block signal §6.2 uses ("block once with the reason"). A SessionStart or PreToolUse hook exiting non-zero is a benign failure; a Stop hook exiting non-zero because it timed out is indistinguishable from a deliberate block, so the safety rule of §6.4 can manufacture exactly the never-finishing agent §6.2 warns against.
suggestion: Make §6.4 kind-aware: the failure exit for a hook whose non-zero code carries semantics (Stop) must be the allow path, not the block path — i.e. the Stop hook exits 0 (allow) on internal error/timeout, and only blocks when it positively evaluated the §3.3 predicate and found it unmet. Add a test alongside 39/43 pinning "Stop hook internal failure allows the stop".

finding: `location_clusters` entries are `{location, roles[], severities[], count}` (line 529) with no definition of the members. `count` could be findings at that location or the number of distinct roles; `severities[]` could be a deduped set or a per-finding array parallel to `roles[]`; neither array's ordering is fixed. Test 28 (line 662) asserts only that a two-role location is grouped, so it does not force a choice. Two engineers write different fixtures for the same input.
suggestion: Define `count` as the number of findings at that location, `roles[]` and `severities[]` as deduped sets in a stated order (e.g. roles in corpus order, severities critical→low), and extend test 28 to assert the exact entry for a location holding two findings from one role and one from another.

finding: Test 47 still asserts unconditionally that "a unit that wrote a valid escalation record stops the run as an escalation whatever exit code the harness returned", but §5.2 now qualifies exactly that sentence with §3.4's precedence, under which the same iteration can record `converged` instead. §10.6 was modified in round 14 (tests 57–58) without carrying the qualifier into test 47, so the test suite pins the pre-repair rule.
suggestion: Amend test 47 to name its precondition (a cycle that is not releasable in that iteration) and add the complement — an escalating unit in an iteration that became releasable records `converged` — so tests 34 and 47 agree with §5.2.

finding: §10.7 enumerates the `tp resume` JSON additions as "`next_units` and `last_failure`", but §4.1 also adds `round` to `tp resume --json`, and test 38 asserts it. Any assertion pinning resume's exact object set therefore also moves for `round`, which the migration note does not cover.
suggestion: Add `round` to §10.7's list of resume shape additions.

finding: §3.1 step 4 says "units marked concurrent together", implying a per-entry marking in `next_units`. §4.1 explicitly denies that surface: "Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table". Two sections describe the same dispatch decision from incompatible sources.
suggestion: Reword step 4 to derive concurrency from the kind: "Spawn a runner process per unit — kinds §3.3 marks parallel together, every other kind alone."

finding: Lines 168-172 require two observable behaviours that no test covers: the inertness of `run_max_budget_usd` is "reported once at run start, not silently", and under a per-kind map "the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered" while the cap accrues only the reporting kinds. Test 11 asserts only `spend: null` and an inert `cap-budget`; test 56 covers per-kind dispatch but not partial accrual.
suggestion: Add a test asserting the run-start report exists and names the unmetered kinds under a mixed per-kind map, and that `totals.spend_usd` accrues only the metered kinds' spend.

finding: Unit ids become path components with no stated sanitization. The log path is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` and the role file is `role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`, while §3.1.1 defines the `audit-fix` id as the finding's `role:item_id` — a value composed from auditor-authored data that can contain `/`, spaces or a leading `.`. A `/` in an `item_id` silently redirects the log write into a non-existent subdirectory (or escapes `TP_RUN_DIR` entirely), and the spec gives the implementer no rule.
suggestion: Specify a sanitization rule for the path-forming use of `id` (e.g. replace every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` with `-`, truncate to a stated length), and state that `TP_UNIT_ID` still carries the unsanitized id so `tp audit --resolve` can select the row by its real key.

finding: §3.5 now pins `tp run --status` at exit 0/3, but §3.4's unchanged enumeration reads as exhaustive for the command — "`tp run` exits 0 on `converged`, 4 on every other `stop_reason`, and 2 on a usage error" — and test 54 pins only 0 and 4. A caller told it can separate outcomes "without parsing the payload" now meets a third code that §3.4 never admits.
suggestion: Add one clause to §3.4 stating that the `--status` and `--dry-run` sub-modes never enter the loop and carry their own codes (§3.5), or move the sub-mode codes into §3.4's enumeration so both sections list the same set.

finding: "when an iteration produces several, the driver reports the lowest `seq` and preserves them all" — but nothing in the run-state schema (§3.5) or the `--status` output holds an escalation path, so "reports" has no destination an implementer can build against. `notify_cmd` receives `TP_ESCALATION_PATH`, which is the only place the path is stated to travel; an operator who did not configure `notify_cmd` gets `stop_reason: escalation` and must find the record by hand.
suggestion: Add `escalation_path` (and optionally `escalation_count`) to the run state and to `tp run --status` output, defined as the record with the lowest `seq`, and state that this is the same value `TP_ESCALATION_PATH` carries.

finding: Line 503 states that under `--compact` `stop_reason` and the cap totals survive while per-unit rows and log paths are stripped. No test in §10 exercises `--compact` on any `tp run` output, so the one field-level output contract §7 adds is unverified. §3.2.1's `TP_RUNNER_SEAM` precedence claim (line 153: outranks every layer including a CLI flag) is likewise asserted by no test — test 1 establishes only that the seam exists.
suggestion: Add a test asserting `tp run --status --compact` keeps `stop_reason` and the cap totals and drops `units[]` and `log_path`, and one asserting the seam wins over an explicit `--runner` CLI flag.

finding: §7 says the new fields are covered by `tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` "on the same terms as every existing workflow field", while the same section carves `notify_cmd` out of the layered path and reads it from `.tp/local.json` only. `--extract` writes overrides into `.tp/config.json`, a layer where `notify_cmd` is by definition never read, and `validate --project` validating a committed `notify_cmd` would bless a value with no effect.
suggestion: Qualify the sentence: `--resolved` reports `notify_cmd` from `.tp/local.json`, `--extract` never emits it, and `validate --project` flags a `notify_cmd` found in `.tp/config.json` as inert. Pin the exclusion in test 16, which today only asserts the read location.
